# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It moves from naming and market to the context, then the window, the problem, my own beliefs about it, the checks on what Keel wrote, and finally who asks and who gets the link, which is how I'd explain Expanse to a stranger.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 put the same context question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), with the window question between them. Screens 11 and 12 both have me check the Importance rows: the reviewed check shows the same card again after the review.
founder.missing: The belief questions (8, 9) only ask about a job failing mid-run, but the bigger half of my problem is the opposite: researchers over-request two to three times and the GPUs sit idle (59% of compute wasted on the cluster we measured). Nothing asked how many researchers pad their requests, or by how much, so the 'without wasting the cluster' half of the job is never put to my own belief. The flow also never asks about the cluster operators who actually pay per cluster, as distinct from the researchers who feel the pain, and it never asks about the solution or the price.

PRIMARY.order_why: The 'which would you most like made easier' screen comes before the screen about how guessing memory, time and GPUs actually went, so I was asked to pick a wish before describing the experience it's about; the counter also shows '1 of 4' on two screens.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the job failed mid-run (out of memory, hit the time limit, or something else), how much work or how many days were lost, and whether I over-request to be safe and how long that makes me wait in the queue.

screens.why3: I know what my users wrestle with around submission from the thread and from our measurement installs, so I can name these difficulties from what they actually do.
screens.why4: Choosing a partition or queue sits at the submit moment, but moving data on and off the cluster and getting software working happen before a job is ready to submit, so two of my three rows sit outside the moment the screen names; the 'I'm not sure' chip fits.
screens.why5: The question restates my circumstance word for word and leaves my rows as typed, so nothing of mine has drifted.
screens.why7: The count is met (three rivals, so with the locked own row a stranger can fill two picks without it), but the card wants every rival at the moment the circumstance names, and data transfer and software setup belong to earlier stages of the work, which bends the moment rule; the review may reword or set them aside.
screens.instead: Same question; rows: Choosing which partition or queue to submit to; Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting; Guessing how long the job will sit in the queue

screens.why1: Right after I named the other difficulties, it makes sense to check my problem and the rivals before they become the words strangers hear.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, GPU-hour allocation and getting software working on the cluster are everyday words to anyone submitting SLURM or K8s jobs.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher on a shared cluster does themselves, so they can answer from last week's submissions.
screens.why4: The own row is three things in one (memory, GPUs and run time), and moving data and getting software working happen before the job is ready to submit rather than at that moment.
screens.why5: My own row is the act I described, sizing memory, GPUs and run time before submitting, and the rivals are the ones I named.
screens.why7: The belief can go either way with four rivals and the own row first and locked, but the own row restates the circumstance ('memory, GPUs and run time have to be guessed') instead of naming the part that goes wrong, and two rivals sit outside the submit moment.
screens.instead: Sizing a job so it neither fails nor wastes GPUs (own) · Choosing which partition or queue to submit to · Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting · Getting the job's environment and modules right before submitting · Setting checkpoints so a killed job can restart

screens.why1: After my Save it is natural to see what Keel's review changed in my list before the stranger hears it, and nothing here is asked twice.
screens.why2: Partition, queue and staging data are everyday words on a SLURM cluster, and every row reads plainly on first reading; only the 'yours + 3' note is terse.
screens.why3: Each row is something my researchers actually wrestle with at submit time on a shared cluster.
screens.why4: Four distinct submit-time difficulties in the trade's words; partition choice touches GPU type, but it is its own decision, not a restatement of sizing.
screens.why5: The own row is my 'guessing memory, time, and GPUs' made into an act, and I saw nothing in the changed rows I needed to put back.
screens.why7: The own row comes first as an -ing act from my problem clause, with three rivals from the same moment, the belief's 'four things' matches the list, and a stranger can pick for or against it.

screens.why1: After the importance check, the last problem question is naturally how researchers size jobs today and how that goes, which is exactly what I'd expect to be asked next.
screens.why2: Guessing memory, GPUs and walltime and padding the request is everyday language on a SLURM cluster; the hint's generic example 'checking for errors by hand' is off-trade but doesn't get in the way.
screens.why3: I know how researchers size jobs and how much they over-request from the measurement data (two to three times), so I answer from what I've seen, not a guess.
screens.why4: The two boxes, one for what they do and one for how it goes, fit my answer, and the single 'I'm not sure' chip is the right way out for a founder.
screens.why5: The question reuses my own job wording ('get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster') and my typed answer and rungs come through unchanged.
screens.why7: My rungs fit the card: one measure (reserved versus used), the first rung working, best to worst. But the screen never asks where 'good enough' ends, so the line falls to a default instead of my placing it, a bend of the card's second-box rule.
screens.instead: How do researchers size a job before submitting today, and what do they size it with? Then: how does it usually turn out, best to worst, and mark the last one you'd still call fine.

screens.why1: Right after I typed how researchers size jobs today, checking the five outcomes Keel drew from it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Ran first time', 'holding three times what it used', 'failed partway and had to be resubmitted' are exactly how researchers on a SLURM cluster talk about a job.
screens.why3: Every researcher knows whether their last job ran, died or sat on idle GPUs, and roughly how much it reserved against what it used, from sacct or the dashboard.
screens.why4: The first three rungs grade idle reservation and the last two grade whether the job finished, so a job that padded 3x and then hit its walltime fits two rungs, and there is a gap between 'about right' and 'about twice'.
screens.why5: My rungs are kept word for word, but the line Keel set under 'holding about twice what it used' counts the 2x over-request as today's way working, when 2-3x padding is the very waste I pitch against.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, five rungs in order with the last a failure, and a balance that can go either way, but rungs 4 and 5 leave the reserved-idle measure for job failure, the same stand-in the card names, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Keep the five but move the line under 'Ran first time, sized about right' so that holding twice, holding three times or more, failing partway and never finishing all count as falling short.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is the natural last step before the link goes out to researchers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but the hint mixes video, voice, credits and a one-time recording in one paragraph, so 'records the voice you pick once for this project: 400 credits' takes me a second read to see that the cost is the same either way.
screens.why3: Which voice should front my study is my own call, and the 5-second previews give me what I need to make it.
screens.why4: There are two distinct interviewers, each with a preview and a default already picked, and the hint's note that people can read and type covers the researchers who won't talk on video, so no option is missing.
screens.why5: Nothing about my product or my roles is touched, and the screen only sets up who reads my questions aloud.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions? (Daphne is picked; tap to hear either. Same cost either way: 400 credits, recorded once.) — Daphne ▶ 5 s / Saskia ▶ 5 s

screens.why1: Once the study is written and the asker chosen, how the researchers answer is the obvious next thing to settle before sending.
screens.why2: Video, typing, tapping and an AI interviewer are plain to a founder selling to ML engineers; the Daphne name is explained in the same line.
screens.why3: I know my researchers live in terminals and Slack and would rather read and tap between job submissions than sit through a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI video, text, or let them choose covers the real choices, each distinct, and my pick Read and tap is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is changed; it addresses researchers and ML engineers exactly as I typed them.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, the obvious last step is who gets the link, and I can only answer it once the study is written.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly who receives a link and who sends it, and 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own screen, which I have just been using.
screens.why3: I know who I would reach, since I asked HN readers and HPC operators by name and could post in a cluster's user channel, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Known people, a Keel search list and one open link for a group cover how I would reach researchers on shared clusters, and the three do not overlap; the Google sign-in on the open link is a detail, not a missing option.
screens.why5: Nothing about Expanse or its roles is changed or leaked here, and my pick of 'people I know by name' is offered as I said it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside 'Frequency: 4 counted', but the 5 needed is only on the card below, and it names Frequency alone when Importance and Current solution are just as short, so I have to read down to see why the page is uncalled.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart; the tally and '6 of 7 · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' read cleanly, but the kicker's '4 TO 7 COUNTED' takes a second look to see it is a range across cards and not one count.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my words, but Prevalence and Frequency became 'had a job fail mid-run', when my belief was that everyone has to guess sizes at every submission and over-requests so jobs mostly don't fail, and that is a different and much harder claim.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more counted answer on three cards, but the screen never says to get more answers, and it says nothing about what holding Prevalence means for Expanse.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and the counts stay visible, 'at the bar' is not dressed up as strong, and the short cards are called too few rather than given a lean.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each have 4 of the 5 counted answers needed, so get at least one more researcher to answer. Prevalence held at 6 of 7, the bar, for 'had to guess memory, GPUs and run time before submitting a job in the last 5 working days', not for 'had a job fail mid-run'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know it held and that it held exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against over 7 people, with my bar marked at 6 on a 0 to 7 axis, so what is counted, out of how many and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the band and the event, but the segment is cut to 'researchers and ML engineers' with no SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100+ GPUs, and the event is only the failure half of my problem: I typed sizing to neither fail nor waste, and 'everyone over-requests' was the part I was sure of.
screens.why_b4: The So line only says it is common and points me to the next two cards; it never says what a mid-run failure in 6 of 7 means for leading with 'runs to the end first time'.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and 'at your bar exactly' keeps the hold from being called strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 researchers on 100+ GPU SLURM/K8s clusters had a job fail mid-run this week, exactly your 8-in-10 bar on a small group, so failures are common enough to lead with 'runs first time'; see Frequency for how often.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (working days out of 5) and over how many (4 counted, 1 empty cell) are plain, but the legend's 'what you said' versus 'at what you said', the bar given as '4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' and both 'median' and 'middle answer' labels took me a second look.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is my dimension and 3 to 5 working days out of 5 is my range, but my belief is about sizing every job at submit time, and 'have a job fail mid-run' is the rarer outcome, so the card counts something narrower than what I meant; 'Asked: Asked:' and the stray '— the most recent time it happened' on a count question read oddly.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that all 4 counted answers fall inside my range, so one more counted answer would decide it, or that I should go and get it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the two uncounted answers are named with their reasons, so nothing is claimed beyond the 4 counted.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted said 3 to 5 working days (middle answer 4), so one more counted answer settles it; send the study to one more researcher who submits jobs most working days.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know where it stands and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 8 picks over 4 people, and my row's 3 stands out, but the bar itself lives only in the strip as 'your bar · 4 of 5', which I first read as '4 counted' and had to work out against the 2-in-3 rule.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension and 'Sizing memory, GPUs and run time' is plainly my problem, but it is not my own row's wording ('Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'), and the actor reads 'Researchers and ML engineers' rather than the people I named.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it never says that 3 of 4 lean my way and that one more counted researcher picking sizing would carry it to 4 of 5, nor what to do with Kwabena's point about data staging and libraries.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the n in view (6 answered, 4 counted, two named as not counted and why) and calls it 'a lean, not a call', claiming nothing past the four people.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 counted put sizing in their two; one more researcher picking it makes 4 of 5 and it holds, so send it to one more, and note that data staging and software versions drew picks too.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The rows, the for/against counts and the line under 'Ran, holding about twice what it used' read at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' looks like a tally next to 3 for and 1 against, and I had to work out that it means 2 in 3 of five people rounded up.
screens.why_b3: It is my act in my words, guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting, for researchers and ML engineers, my segment, under the Current solution name, with my own rung named at the line.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that 3 of the 4 counted already fell short, or that one more counted answer below my line would decide it.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know the verdict and why at once.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the belief says 'Sizing memory, GPUs and run time' where the item I checked now reads 'Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs': recognisable, but not my current words.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more counted answer, but nothing says so plainly or says what the lone against-voice means for the idea.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's an obvious check that I'm the right person: I submit jobs to a shared GPU cluster, and the size cut makes sense even though the kicker's 'A recent time' doesn't quite match a standing yes-or-no.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, cluster and GPUs are my everyday words, and it's one short question I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know I submit to our SLURM cluster, but I'd have to guess whether it crosses 100 GPUs, since I see my partition and quota rather than the whole cluster's count.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a gate, and per the rules a gate has no escape, so none is missing.
screens.why5: It names my setup in plain trade terms and says nothing about a product or the founder's plan.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to say, and 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is a bit stiff next to the screener's plain 'Yes or no.' but still easy to hold.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs in total? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I submit to a big SLURM or Kubernetes cluster, asking whether a job died mid-run in the last week is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: 'Fail mid-run' is how I'd say it myself, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly which of my jobs died this week; it's in my squeue and sacct history and my inbox.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the chips beside it belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed because I under-requested memory, GPUs or time, but 'fail mid-run' also takes in crashes from my own bugs, NCCL hangs and node failures, so the meaning has drifted wider than what was typed.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no.' is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Two fixed answers on the founder's event, no escape, and someone whose jobs all ran to the end can truly say No, so the band can be both supported and refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a job killed mid-run for hitting its memory or time limit? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to a job failing mid-run this week, asking on how many of those days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Job", "fail mid-run" and "working days" are exactly how I talk about my SLURM runs, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week my jobs died partway through, because I was the one resubmitting them and checking the logs.
screens.why4: 1 to 5 covers every possible count of days after a yes at the gate, with no overlap, and "I can't recall" fits someone who runs many jobs a day.
screens.why5: It asks the same failure I was asked about at the gate, with no product, company or role name showing through; "fail mid-run" is broader than an out-of-memory or time-limit kill, but it is the founder's own clause.
screens.why6: Short and one question, and "a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall" is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of working days from 1 to the window's 5 in order, with no 0 and the single cant_recall escape; the founder's low isn't shown to me, but 1 to 5 can split for and against any low of 2 or more.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often my jobs died mid-run, it makes sense to ask which pre-submit headache I'd most want fixed.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, staging data and sizing memory and GPUs are everyday words on a SLURM cluster, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I do myself before I hit sbatch, so I can answer from my last run.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and real, but 'Sizing memory, GPUs and run time' bundles three guesses into one row, and 'partition or queue' is two words for one choice.
screens.why5: The founder's hurt is under-requesting so the job gets killed mid-run, but 'Sizing memory, GPUs and run time' just restates the guessing step and drops the 'so it doesn't die' part that actually costs me days.
screens.why6: Four short parallel options and one escape at the end are easy to hold by ear, though the last two run close to a mouthful.
screens.why7: The own item is present, not first, with three rivals and None of these at the first ask, but the own row is a list inside one option and reads as the circumstance said again rather than the part that goes wrong.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Choosing which partition to submit to · Sizing a job's resources so it isn't killed mid-run · Matching software versions before submitting · Working out which data to stage first · None of these

screens.why1: After the frequency and the which-step-hurts questions, asking how sizing my last job actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say 'requested' or 'asked for', not 'holding', and 'twice what it used' doesn't say which resource, so I'd read it twice to work out whether it means memory, time or GPUs.
screens.why3: I sized my last job myself and seff tells me what it used, but my memory might be twice over while the time was about right, so I'd be averaging three resources into one answer.
screens.why4: 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' and 'Never ran to the end' overlap, since a job killed mid-run never ran to the end either; there's also a gap between 'about right' and 'about twice', where a 1.5x over-request has no clear home; I can't recall fits a job I sized myself.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or tool leaks, and the under-requesting failure I care about is in there in plain cluster terms.
screens.why6: The stem lists three resources in one breath, and 'ran, holding three times or more what it used' is a mouthful to hold while the last two options are read.
screens.why7: There's a working first rung, five rungs in order, a line under a working rung and the right escape, but rungs 2-3 grade idle reservation while rungs 4-5 switch to whether the job finished, which is exactly the measure mix the card warns against.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did what you requested compare with what it used? -- About right, and it finished · About double what it used · Three times or more what it used · Too little, killed and resubmitted · Too little, never finished at all; or I can't recall
